First heard calling 30 feet north of the trail at: (37.8673771, -122.3102690), making squeaky Song Sparrow like bark calls, with single barks at first, followed by often double or triple barks. The bird later also gave the typical WIWR chatter call, similar to the recording in the Sibley app. The bird then came close, first giving good views in the willow clump on the north side of the trail at (37.8671807, -122.3103444), then crossing to the willow thicket at the southeast corner of the intersection of the main trail and the small spur trail (in the same spot where I found the first county record in 2024). Eventually moved south to (37.8664338, -122.3103592), before popping up again near the original location on the north side of the main trail. Last heard at 8:40am at about (37.8672398, -122.3105439). Pale overall, with a distinctly whitish throat and textured pale coloration extending across the entire side of the face, including the auriculars. The whitish pebbled/scaled texture extended downward from the throat, through the lower breast and upper flanks. The lower flanks were barred with dark blackish interspersed with thin white bands. Whitish supercilium, with a medium brown line extending rearward from the eye. The medium brown crown and nape merged with a brown to chestnut back and a short chestnut tail with dark barring. Tiny white spangles on the lesser and median wing coverts, brown and buff barring on the primaries. When brightly lit, the upper parts appeared almost rufous in color. This is purely speculative, but given that this bird was observed in the same location (sometimes perching in nearly identical spots in the same willows), this could be the same returning individual that I found in November, 2024 and which continued through March 2025. Interestingly, that bird had a distinctive depigmented (mostly white) left alula. Unfortunately, my photos didn't capture that feature well on the current bird. The 2024 bird was later accepted by CBRC ( a first record for the county), but was not detected in the winter of 2025/2026. See https://ebird.org/checklist/S203502632 for the 2024 observation. Briefly in bare plum at base of hill below the Randall Museum garden, I was standing approximately here: 37.76410, -122.43736. Tine of observation was 7:40-45. Was sorting through the Sparrow flock on the lawn when I saw a bird with very pale underparts  perch up in the branches of the plum. before getting a look at it with my binoculars my first thought was Eastern Phoebe. I got it in my bins for approximately 3 to 5 seconds at no more than 20 m distant.. flycatcher by shape and posture, sayornis by dipping tail. The underparts, which is what first grabbed my attention were very not whitish with a light yellow/cream wash, from the belly through breast to throat. Upper parts were a dark gray, paler than a black Phoebe. The bird never called and took off when a Cooper’s Hawk landed in the eucalyptus tree above the lawn. Spent the next hour and a half trying to relocate it,  doing laps from the Lawn to  the Museum garden. this is the first record of eastern Phoebe for Corona Hill. While rare,  sightings of the species are not unprecedented in late fall through early winter. One was  on Twin Peaks on 11/19-23/25. Perhaps a thorough search of the park later in the day will turn it up again.

A spectacular and ferocious-looking Mesoamerican megavireo initially at (37.7329629, -122.4987988), first in the madrone (?) outside the fence and then in the oak inside the Grizzle Bear enclosure. A short time later we had a Yellow-green Vireo 300 m away in shrubs around (37.7336260, -122.5014907), presumably the same individual; it was quite mobile and hard to stay on. A very large vireo, almost the size of a Hermit Thrush, with wings drooped and tail cocked, an immense bill and large head, bright greenish-yellow dorsum except for light blue-gray cap, highlighter yellow flanks and sides of chest, whitish strip including throat and extending down underparts, whitish supercilium, indistinct dark eyeline and lateral crown stripes. We missed photos the first time we saw this bird, despite decent looks for all three observers, but managed to photograph it the second time. Another rather strong year for this species in California; this is the ~8th in NorCal this year.

BCC!!!!!!!! Unbelievably electric to see an exquisite Mexican pine-loving mountain microwarbler in riparian at Pescadero Marsh. A stunning bird at (37.2577725, -122.3950345), in an arroyo willow when I found it at about 1:30 pm. It was initially quite cooperative and allowed a couple minutes of excellent views and reasonably good photos. I lost the bird while getting word out, but it was refound and seen briefly by Chris Hayward, Malia DeFelice, and others high in pines at the same location about an hour later, and then refound again by Cédric Duhalde and seen by many others later in the day, after I had to leave. 

This is a first for San Mateo County and is the c. 8th record for NorCal (excluding records from the mountains of Tulare and Mono), following two from Monterey, two from Santa Cruz, two from SF (one of them being from SEFI), and one from Mendocino. Of these, three (1 MTY, 1 SF, 1 MEN) wintered or attempted to winter; the remaining four were fall migrants, spanning the dates 9/6 (a one-day MTY migrant) to 10/15 (the second day of the two-day stay of the migrant record from SEFI). The wintering SF bird returned on 9/19 last year. Given the late date of this record and the excellent habitat for a wintering Grace's at this location—a nice big stand of pines, including large mature ones and some denser younger ones, near riparian—there is a reasonable chance that this bird may attempt to winter.

Continuing second state record. About 11a.m. on 22 Oct., Marty Freeland found a Yellow-browed Warbler in Moss Beach. I went as soon as I could, which was about 24 hours later, arriving shortly before 3p.m. on Oct. 23rd. To describe the location briefly, at this location there is a small, rectangular, dirt parking lot, bounded on the southeast and southwest sides by willows. There is a small bridge through the willows that connects the parking lot to a paddock or sand school just southeast of the parking lot. The sand school is bounded on the north edge by the same clump of willows; maybe 200 feet of them. At about 3:30, I heard the surprisingly loud call of the Yellow-browed Warbler from the willows near the bridge.About 20 people congregated, but we did not see the bird, so I walked around to the other side of that willow clump to look, where Paul Saraceni had been standing since my arrival. Soon after walking up next to Paul (who if I remember correctly, had also heard the bird call), he exclaimed that he had the bird and quickly put me on it. Thank you, Paul! The bird was fairly frantic, with a similar activity level to a kinglet, and remained in the highest shady branches of the willows for about 5 minutes. Thus it allowed me a number of very brief views. It then flew southwestward, and was soon relocated when only a couple minutes later called loudly three times in rapid succession. I then got two nice—but fleeting—looks of it on a sunny willow branch, before it flew off north and I left a bit after 4:00. 
	The call was a shockingly loud, thin call. It fell in pitch at the start and rose towards the end, and was reminiscent of the “suweep!” of a Western Flycatcher. Visually, this was a small, kinglet-sized bird that appeared overall a dull green or pale gray. To me it appeared greenish above and pale below, with a short and stubby bill. It had a bold and prominent pale supercilium that extended from the lores back well behind the eye, a palish wingbar (I was told there were two, but my views only sufficient to see one), and perhaps a paler and slightly contrasting throat. I have seen very few Phylloscopus sp. in my life; including Dusky, Willow, and Wood. If I were to compare this bird to a Wood Warbler, I would describe it as duller green overall; shorter billed and winged, i.e., closer to the shape of a kinglet; and with a wingbar. That is all I was able to gather visually. Obviously, the call is distinctive.
	An excellent find by Marty, and fantastic redemption for me, as I was one of many chasers present on the October Saturday in Markleeville when that Yellow-browed Warbler was not seen. Coincidences are fun, and here is one: each state record of Yellow-browed Warbler was found on a Thursday, continued on the Friday, and was gone on the Saturday. Each Yellow-browed Warbler stakeout was also during irruptions of montane finches, and there were a number of crossbills on both occasions. Although there were many Evening Grosbeaks in Markleeville, and none for me in Moss Landing.

This was a nice North American bird for Tom.

Very faithful to the willow patch at (37.5245820, -122.5039200), seen pretty much continually from ~7:20 until around 08:50, then again from 09:45 to 10:15. 

Behavior very mobile, even moreso than a Kinglet. Constantly in motion, hardly ever pausing for more than a second before resuming flitting and gleaning. For those hoping for photos - track it with your camera. It *will* move in the time it takes to switch from binoculars to camera.

Outstanding find by Marty Freeland! A small, grayish-green, kinglet-like warbler with a small bill with some yellow, a long, pale, high-contrast supercilium, and two wing bars. It gave occasional high-pitched “suweet” calls as it foraged frantically deep in the willows, making looping flycatching sallies. Possibly the worst photos of the m.ob.

LFM notes: astoundingly small and fast-moving, even more so than RCKI. While superficially kinglet-like, this bird stood out as more "long" than "round", with paler underparts, and an obvious pale eyebrow, mostly white and maybe slightly yellow toward forehead. Upperparts had some distinct greenish yellow, and also showed a dark "kinglet bar" behind the second white wingbar. In certain binocular views at certain angles, the auricular appeared somewhat stippled and the pale throat looked lightly streaked with dark gray. Lower mandible of bill about 2/3s pale orange at the base. Legs pale. Foraging behavior frantic, rarely sitting still for more than a couple seconds. Often would drop and do a looping flycatching maneuver, circling quickly back up to the spot it left. Calls heard were a joyous, whistled "su-weet!" slightly reminiscent of Western Flycatcher, sometimes while foraging but definitely the few times it flew between willow patches.

The presence of two wingbars eliminates many Phylloscopus. The possible similar species would be Two-barred (would show longer tail, larger more obvious orangey bill, and would lack "kinglet bar"), Hume's Leaf-Warbler (would be duller, with darker bill and legs), and Pallas's Leaf-Warbler (would have much bolder head pattern with median crown stripe, and smaller bill). The call heard numerous times also helps eliminate many other possible species.

Epic find reported to Telegram group by Marty Freeland at 11:31am. I gobbled a sandwich, donned my riding gear, assayed the weather conditions, and hit the road at 11:59. Patchy rain and mist prevailed but did not slow me; I merged onto Highway 1 in HMB at 12:59 (record time for that leg) and reached at the specified GPS location (37.524732596260996, -122.50388501558992) at 1:19pm. I had glimpses within five minutes of my arrival and bettered my views through the next two hours. The bird stuck to the top half of the willows, constantly flitting, on both sides of the small clearing. It periodically escaped the mob's collective gaze but would invariably resurface within thirty yards; it was never unaccounted for more than ~15 mins in the time I was present. 

Small-to-medium Phylloscopus warbler with broad, creamy eyeline and wing bars (two) to match. Small, orange-based bill; gray crown without obvious median stripe; crisp, sooty line through eye. Upper back olive-brown; primaries and lower back with a hint of yellow. Flanks and belly creamy-gray, perhaps with a very light yellow cast (though it was tough to see with the bird backlit, against the sky for much of my vigil). Tail gray and without any white. The wing bars rule out Dusky, Arctic, and Kamchatka Leaf Warblers; Pallas's Leaf Warbler is smaller with yellow lines on head/face an an obvious pale rump.  A quick, upsweeping two syllable 'suwee' call, given at long intervals, eliminated Hume's and Two-barred. Bay Area bike bird #376. San Mateo County bike bird #310. The attached image is a back-of-camera snap of an image captured by Ryan Mense. I didn;t take my camera on account of the extra weight and the possibility for rain damage while riding. Bird was too fast/small for a digi-binoc.

While scoping to the N just beyond the surfers in the rear surf @ 9:25, a dark shearwater suddenly entered my field of view heading S low over the water then arcing up and down over the swells repeatedly. It was in my scope view for just under a minute as it continued heading S until out of view. As it was not very far out and there was no sun glare in the overcast conditions, I had excellent views as it went up and down over the swells. Rather dark upperparts and underparts, including an almost uniform underwing without contrasty white flash. In scope views its head looked short and rounded, almost fulmar-like (it was not a fulmar with its shearwater bill and wing structure). What really stood out to me was its rather buoyant, light flight and arcing over the waves on a morning with not much wind -- different to my eyes than the flight-style of Sooties. Also interesting that it was a solo individual, much closer to shore than I usually observe shearwaters from this seawatch. The last Sooties from the seawatch were back on 9/28.

An amazing experience with a moderately dull bird, initially at (37.7702658, -122.4763537). It then worked east along the lakeshore halfway to the concrete bridge before flying north across the street to the thick stuff at the top of the Log Cabin Trail hill, where I lost it. It was then not seen until Dario refound it at sunset back in the lakeside willows, which I would imagine are the best place to look. It was giving a loud, sweet, slightly breathy chip, kind of like a weaker California Towhee, intermediate in quality between Hooded and Orange-crowned warblers. 

A very large warbler, mainly rich saturated yellow in color with a white crissum and slate-blue wings and tail, duller yellow on the face and above grading into greenish-yellow on the back, large eye and bill on otherwise blank face (maybe slightly dusky lores?), a rather blank facial expression, striking undertail pattern slightly reminiscent of Magnolia, mainly white from the underside with black tips/edges, forming an interesting pattern when spread. Very little white visible from above, suggesting HY (in combination with its also being rather dull), but views and photos did not permit seeing whether white was limited to the three outermost rectrices or not. Cooperative when in lakeside willows and rather slow-moving. I first saw its face staring me down, and seeing the bright yellow face of a medium, large-billed, blank-faced passerine, it looked almost like an Orchard Oriole. And then a microsecond later it looked obviously like a Prothonotary Warbler and tripled my heart rate and all that! This was my first self-found Protho and my most wanted self-find (proportional to actual rarity) in the state and an absolutely electric experience. Photos.

Resident birds. Rare in the county but now established here and breeding. This small flock was perched in a willow tree here  37.247840416807094, -121.87044567976321 and was making frequent trips down into the reeds and grasses to gather food, offering great views. 5 of the birds were adults but interestingly there were 3 juvenile birds hidden in the willow tree giving begging calls and fluttering their wings. They were pretty young (some yellow still showing on their gapes and unscaled buffy breasts) which seems weird for this late in the season (possibly a second or third brood?). The birds were flying down into the grass and bringing seeds back to their young. ID: Small finch-like birds; reddish brown overall with large conical black bills and black scaling on the breast. Juveniles were similar to adults but lacked the patterning on the underside and still had some fluff on their heads. Photos + audio to follow.
